name: Nickel metal from laterite or pentlandite
note: Nickel isolation is stubborn; the key advance is roasting laterite with charcoal at 1300-1600C to form volatile nickel oxide, then reduction with carbon monoxide. Pentlandite (nickel-iron sulfide) smelts to matte, concentration by repeated roasting and reduction.

name: Cobalt metal from smaltite and erythrite
note: Cobalt ores (arsenides and carbonates) must be roasted to destroy arsenic before reduction. The reduced metal is brittle; the discovery is that repeated roasting and reduction cycles improve malleability. German smalt production inadvertently separated cobalt this way.

name: Manganese metal from pyrolusite
note: Pyrolusite reduction with carbon proceeds via intermediate manganese oxides; the trick is controlling temperature to prevent re-oxidation. Electrolytic reduction of manganese sulfate was later; aluminothermic reduction (Goldschmidt process) became dominant by 1920.

name: Chromium from chromite ore
note: Chromite (FeO.Cr2O3) requires aluminothermic reduction; carbon reduction produces brittle chromium carbide, not ductile metal. The 1900s Goldschmidt process made chromium practical. Chromium is critical to stainless steel but extraction was slow.

name: Tungsten from wolframite and scheelite
note: Tungsten ores must be roasted to tungstate (WO3), then reduced with hydrogen at high temperature to avoid carbide formation. The metal is extremely refractory; ductility comes only from careful hydrogen reduction and then hydrogen firing. Siemens and Coolidge's work in 1900s-1910s made tungsten wire possible.

name: Molybdenum from molybdenite
note: Molybdenite (MoS2) roasts to MoO3, then hydrogen reduction to metal. The key breakthrough is that molybdenum carbides are hard but brittle; pure reduction avoids carbides. Used in high-speed tool steel from ~1910 onward.

name: Vanadium from carnotite and vanadinite
note: Vanadium ores are roasted to vanadium pentoxide (V2O5), then reduced. Vanadium steel (from Peru deposits) strengthens high-carbon steel dramatically. Henry Ford's 1908 Model T used vanadium steel axles, knowledge obtained from French metallurgists. Pre-1908 extraction was purely small-batch.

name: Titanium from rutile and ilmenite
note: Titanium dioxide (TiO2) is extremely stable; reduction is late 1940s with chlorination to TiCl4 then magnesium reduction. Before 1950, titanium metal exists only in laboratory quantities. The extreme affinity for oxygen and nitrogen makes it exceptionally difficult; Kroll process post-WWII changed everything.

name: Magnesium metal from seawater and mineral salts
note: Magnesium is isolated by precipitating MgCl2 from seawater as Mg(OH)2, dissolving in HCl, then electrolyzing molten magnesium chloride (fused salt electrolysis). Dow process (1916) made electrolytic extraction practical. Earlier, magnesium came from Epsom salt reduction - tiny scale.

name: Rare earth elements as a group from monazite
note: Rare earths are nearly inseparable by fractional crystallization because their ionic radii are too similar. Monazite sand contains 50+ ppm but extracting one pure element from cerium, lanthanum, and a dozen others requires 500+ crystallization cycles. Industrial rare earth chemistry barely existed before 1950; treated as a chemical curiosity.

name: Platinum group metals from alluvial and ore sources
note: Platinum, palladium, rhodium, and iridium occur together; selective dissolution and precipitation is the path. Wollaston's selective aqua regia dissolution (1800s) separated palladium and platinum. Complete separation came slowly; before 1900 most platinum was crude.

name: Uranium and thorium from pitchblende and monazite
note: Uranium oxide (U3O8) dissolves in sulfuric acid; thorium oxide in concentrated HCl. Radioactive decay was discovered in uraninite; Marie Curie's polonium and radium work boosted this field. Before 1920, milligram quantities; WWII urgency drove industrial extraction.

name: Zinc metal by retort distillation from calamine
note: Calamine (zinc silicate/carbonate) mixed with charcoal heats to 1100-1200C in clay retorts; zinc vapor condenses and runs to ingots. The vapor pressure of zinc is crucial: too cool it solidifies in the retort, too hot it escapes. Indian and Chinese retort zinc was known by 1400s; European adoption after 1620.

name: Zinc metal by electrolytic refining of zinc sulfate
note: Sphalerite (zinc sulfide) roasts to ZnO, leaches in sulfuric acid to ZnSO4, electrowinning deposits pure zinc cathode. Electrorefining reduces impurities (cadmium, iron) far better than retort. Competitive by 1900, dominant by 1920.

name: Copper smelting in reverberatory furnace
note: Reverberatory furnace reflects flame off the roof onto ore; no direct contact with fuel. Reduces fuel consumption by half vs. earlier open hearth. The flame path control is the innovation; adopted widely 1700-1800 for both copper and tin.

name: Copper converter: blowing air through molten matte
note: Oxidizing blown air through copper matte burns out iron and sulfur, concentrating copper. Bessemer converter adapted to copper work; timing and oxygen control are critical. Later electric furnaces did this better but converter was dominant 1870-1920.

name: Copper metal by electrowinning from leached ore
note: Leach copper ore in sulfuric acid or use converter blister copper in spent electrolyte; electrowinning deposits ultra-pure copper cathode. Impurities settle as anode slime (source of gold, silver, selenium). Energy-intensive but produces superior purity. Porphyry copper ores (low grade, high volume) demand this technology.

name: Parkes process: removing silver from lead by zinc
note: Cooling molten lead-silver with zinc metal; zinc forms compounds with silver and floats out as dross. Ingenious phase diagram exploitation. Parkes (1850s) solved silver-lead separation; pre-then silver had to stay with lead. Without this, lead refining fails.

name: Electrorefining: purifying crude metal via anode dissolution
note: Crude metal as anode dissolves selectively; pure metal plates on cathode. Impurities less noble than the metal sink as anode slime; impurities more noble do not dissolve. Copper, nickel, lead all purify this way. Wollaston and others developed it; became essential by 1900.

name: Basic Bessemer converter for steel from iron-ore matte
note: Steel converter lined with magnesia/limestone removes phosphorus by forming phosphate slag that floats. Bessemer process (1856) used acid linings and failed on phosphorus; Thomas-Gilchrist (1878) basic lining solved high-phosphorus iron. Enabled use of minette ore and domestic iron worldwide.

name: Induction furnace for high-quality alloy steel
note: AC current through a coil induces eddy currents in metal charge, heating without fuel. No fuel impurities, better composition control. Developed ~1900; expensive until WW1 demand drove production. Allows vacuum melting alloys later.

name: Sintering: fusing powder ore by heating without melting
note: Fine ore particles heat to 0.7-0.9 of melting point; solid-state diffusion bonds particles into a porous cake. Accelerates roasting before smelting and improves furnace throughput. Ancient practice; industrialized in 1900s.

name: Pelletising: forming ore fines into uniform balls
note: Fine ore mixed with binder (bentonite, lime) rolled into pellets; drying and light roasting harden them. Allows use of mill tailings and waste. Improves furnace permeability and reduces dust. Industrial pellet plants ~1920s.

name: Froth flotation: separating sulfide ore minerals by hydrophobic bonding
note: Finely ground ore suspended in water with collector (xanthate); air bubbles preferentially attach sulfides via hydrophobic interaction. Froth overflows carrying ore; tailings sink. Replaces heavy metals gravity separation. Patented Elmore (1899); became standard 1900-1920 for copper, lead, zinc.

name: Cyanidation: leaching gold and silver with CN solution
note: Cyan solutions form soluble gold-cyano and silver-cyano complexes; heap leaching extracts low-grade ore (0.1-1 g/ton). Displacement by zinc powder recovers precious metals. Soluble in 1880s; industrial scale in South Africa 1900+. Replaced amalgamation for low-grade ores.

name: Amalgamation: extracting precious metals with mercury
note: Mercury dissolves gold and silver; panning, shaking table, or mill rotors coat ore with Hg. Later heating drives off Hg and recovers metal. Spanish New World silver (Potosi) relied on this for 300 years. Toxic and inefficient on low-grade ore, displaced by cyanide.

name: Chemical leaching: dissolving ore in sulfuric or nitric acid
note: Heap or vat leaching dissolves ore in acid solution (CuSO4 for copper, FeSO4 for others). Solid residue filtered; solution concentrated and metal recovered by displacement or electrolysis. Industrial scale for copper, nickel from laterite by 1920.

name: Precipitation: recovering metal from solution by chemical reduction
note: Metal ions in solution precipitated by adding a more reactive metal: copper sulfate + iron nail -> metallic copper + ferrous sulfate. Cementation ancient; scale and selectivity improved in 1800s. Used for final recovery from dilute solutions.

name: Vacuum melting: reducing oxygen and gas content in alloys
note: Melting under vacuum removes dissolved oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen. Deoxidizing with aluminum and calcium then vacuum refining produces ultra-clean steel. WW1 prompted research for superior alloys; post-1920 in Germany and US for aircraft.

name: Powder metallurgy: forming shapes from metal powder by sintering
note: Atomize metal or ore into powder, press into shape, sinter to consolidate. Avoids casting defects and enables compositional control. Pre-1950 mostly used for tungsten filaments, carbide tools, and bearing metals. Systematic process metallurgy ~1920s.

name: Austenite formation by heating iron-carbon above critical temperature
note: Steel heated above A3 temperature (800-900C) transforms to austenite, a high-carbon solid solution of iron. The iron-carbon phase diagram is the map: austenite is the single-phase region where carbon is soluble. Quenching from austenite traps high-carbon at low temperature - martensite.

name: Water quenching: rapid cooling of austenite to form martensite
note: Immersing hot steel in water cools it so fast that carbon atoms cannot diffuse; martensite forms - high hardness, high brittleness. Too fast causes cracks; too slow forms pearlite (soft). Medieval smiths knew empirically; Reaumur systematized it 1700s.

name: Oil quenching: slower cooling than water, fewer cracks
note: Oil cools slower than water but faster than air; reduces cracking while still forming martensite. Oil has higher boiling point so cooling is steadier. Luxury until petroleum products became cheap; then standard for high-carbon tools and weapon blades.

name: Brine quenching: salt water for intermediate cooling rate
note: Salt solution (5-10%) increases boiling point and wetting vs. pure water; intermediate cooling rate. Ancient practice, still used. Hygroscopicity minimizes oxide scale. Cheaper than oil, used where higher hardness acceptable.

name: Tempering: controlled reheating to reduce brittleness of martensite
note: Reheating quenched steel to 100-600C softens martensite slightly; some carbon precipitates as cementite, reducing internal stress. Color indicates temperature: pale straw at 225C, dark blue at 300C. Smiths used color empirically for centuries; control improved by thermometers.

name: Carburising: enriching surface carbon content by heating in carbon-rich medium
note: Low-carbon steel in contact with charcoal at 900-950C; carbon diffuses 1-3mm deep. Quenching produces hard case over tough core. Blister steel technique adapted; allows use of wrought iron for tools. Medieval armor makers knew this; systematic use 1600s+.

name: Nitriding: hardening surface by heating in ammonia or nitrogen
note: Heating steel in ammonia gas at 500-600C; nitrogen atoms diffuse into surface forming nitrides (iron nitrides, alloy nitrides). Hardness without need for quenching. Discovered Porsche/Fry ~1912; used for bearing races, gears. Lower temperature than carburising.

name: Induction hardening: localized heating by eddy currents for rapid quenching
note: High-frequency AC through a coil heats steel to austenite temperature in seconds; quench water immediately cools it. Only selected areas harden (gear teeth, bearing races). Eliminates distortion from long heating. German development ~1910; became standard by 1930.

name: Age hardening: precipitation hardening in aluminum-copper alloys
note: Wilm's 1906 accident: naturally aged aluminum-copper alloy (duralumin) hardened slowly over days. Solution heat-treat above 500C dissolves copper; quench traps supersaturated phase; aging at room or moderate temperature precipitates ultra-fine copper particles, hardening dramatically. Explains why old rivets on aircraft got harder.

name: Annealing: controlled heating and slow cooling to soften and relieve stress
note: Heating steel to just below critical temperature, holding, then slow cooling in furnace. Allows recrystallization and grain growth; softens cold-worked metal. Permitting in blacksmithing ancient; systematic control with thermometers by 1850.

name: Normalising: cooling from above critical point in still air for uniform structure
note: Heating to austenite then air cooling (not furnace cooling like annealing). Refines grain and improves mechanical properties compared to as-cast structure. Intermediate between annealing and water quenching. Became standard 1850s onward.

name: Grain size control: understanding how grain size affects mechanical properties
note: Fine grains improve impact strength and ductility; coarse grains improve high-temperature strength. Grain size controlled by austenitizing temperature and cooling rate. Metallography (etching and microscopy) revealed grain structure; Hall-Petch relation became clear by 1950.

name: Work hardening: increasing hardness by plastic deformation at low temperature
note: Cold rolling, drawing, or bending deforms crystal lattice; dislocation density increases, material hardens. Annealing relieves the hardness (recrystallization). Smiths used this for centuries (hammer hardening, cold drawing wire); systematic study in 1900s.

name: Recrystallisation: formation of new strain-free grains during annealing
note: Heating cold-worked metal above recrystallization temperature; new grains nucleate and consume old strained grains. Restores ductility. Temperature depends on metal and prior deformation. Discovery by Ewing and Rosenhain ~1900; mechanism still unclear pre-1950.

name: Tensile testing: measuring yield, ultimate strength, and elongation
note: Pulling a standard sample until fracture; stress and strain measured. Yield point marks end of elasticity; ultimate strength is maximum load. Elongation and reduction of area show ductility. Universal testing machine (Tinius Olsen, 1880s) made this practical; essential for quality control.

name: Charpy impact test: measuring toughness by pendulum impact
note: Notched specimen hit by swinging pendulum; energy absorbed measured by height of rebound. Shows brittle vs. ductile transition with temperature. Charpy (1901) developed it for ship steel; reveals low-temperature brittleness of high-carbon steels and cold-worked materials.

name: Izod impact test: vertical notched-bar impact measurement
note: Similar to Charpy but different specimen geometry and impact geometry. Izod (1903) developed it as competitor to Charpy. Both reveal toughness; Charpy became more standard. Different results due to specimen constraint; both useful for comparison.

name: Brinell hardness test: measuring hardness by indentation size
note: Forcing a hardened ball into material under fixed load; hardness is load divided by indentation surface area. Brinell (1900) developed it; simple and non-destructive (vs. tensile test). Becomes less accurate for very hard materials; superseded by Vickers.

name: Rockwell hardness test: rapid hardness by indentation depth
note: Depth of indentation under fixed load, converted to hardness scale. Multiple scales (A, B, C, etc.) for different materials. Rockwell (1919) developed it; faster than Brinell, direct numerical readout. Requires calibration; became industrial standard by 1930s.

name: Vickers hardness test: pyramid indentation for micro-hardness
note: Diamond pyramid indenter; hardness from diagonal length measured under microscope. Vickers (1925) developed it; measures very small volumes (micro-hardness of individual phases and hardness of thin cases). Supersedes Brinell for precision work.

name: Fatigue testing: measuring S-N curve and stress-life endurance
note: Cyclically loading specimen until fracture; plotting stress vs. number of cycles to failure. Wohler (1850s) began this; revealed that failure occurs below ultimate strength if cycled. Machine development (rotating beam, hydraulic) enabled systematic study. Critical for railways and machinery.

name: Creep testing: measuring time-dependent deformation at elevated temperature
note: Holding constant load at high temperature; measuring deformation over hours or days. Metals deform slowly under stress even below yield point. Essential for high-temperature engines, turbines, boilers. Andrade (1910s) studied primary, secondary, tertiary creep regimes.

name: Metallography: etching polished sections to reveal microstructure
note: Polishing metal smooth, etching with acid or ferric chloride to reveal grain boundaries and phases. Different phases etch differently; comparing etched microstructure to mechanical properties linked them. Sorby (1860s) began this; became routine by 1900.

name: X-ray diffraction: determining crystal structure and lattice parameters
note: X-rays scattered by crystal lattice planes create diffraction pattern; measuring angles and intensities reveals atomic spacing and crystal structure. Bragg (1912) developed the theory; made clear that ferrite is BCC, austenite is FCC. Industrial quantitative use ~1930s.

name: Industrial radiography: X-ray and gamma-ray inspection for internal flaws
note: X-rays pass through metal; dense defects (cracks, porosity) show as dark areas on film. Used for castings and welds. Gamma radiography (radioactive source) came later. Pre-1950 mostly X-ray; excellent for finding shrinkage cavities and cold shut defects.

name: Magnetic particle inspection: revealing surface and near-surface defects
note: Magnetizing part and applying ferrous particles; defects distort field and trap particles, revealing crack patterns. Non-destructive, fast, inexpensive. Developed 1920s; by 1930s standard for forgings and welds. Only works on ferromagnetic materials.

name: Dye penetrant inspection: revealing surface cracks in all materials
note: Penetrating colored or fluorescent liquid into surface cracks, wiping surface, then developer powder highlights cracks. Works on non-magnetic materials (aluminum, stainless). Developed 1940s; became standard post-WW2 for aircraft inspection.

name: Ultrasonic testing: detecting internal flaws by sound reflection
note: High-frequency sound (ultrasound) propagates through metal; internal flaws reflect signal. Measuring reflection time and amplitude reveals flaw location and size. Supersonic flaw detector (1940s) early version. Post-1950 standard for thick sections and welds.

name: Gunmetal: copper-tin-zinc alloy for cannons and bearings
note: 90% Cu, 9% Sn, 1% Zn (approximate). Stronger than pure bronze, better for pressure vessels and bearings. Bell makers used similar alloys; gunmetal formalization came with artillery demand. Redeemed scrap metal by adjusting composition.

name: Bell metal: high-tin bronze for resonance
note: 80% Cu, 20% Sn. High tin content increases brittleness but improves acoustic resonance. Casting is critical: pouring temperature, cooling rate affect tone. Bell founders kept recipes secret; quality varied wildly. Scientific understanding came late (1800s).

name: Speculum: high-tin bronze for telescope mirrors
note: 65% Cu, 35% Sn. Extremely brittle but reflective and polishable to optical surfaces. Herschel used speculum mirrors in telescopes (1780s+). Difficult to cast large mirrors without porosity. Later silver-coated glass replaced it; speculum persisted in cheaper telescopes.

name: Pewter: tin-lead-copper for tableware and drinking vessels
note: Medieval and later standard for drinking vessels (safer than lead-only). Composition controlled by guild (high tin was luxury, high lead was economical). Lead content caused concern; tin-only pewter was expensive. Plating and polishing to gray sheen standard.

name: Solder: lead-tin for joining metals by melting
note: 50-50 lead-tin (eutectic at 183C, flows freely). Earlier solders higher tin (expensive) or higher lead (weak). Eutectic composition discovery ~1800; enabled consistent joints. Tin-only (lead-free) solder came much later due to brittleness.

name: Babbitt: tin-antimony-copper bearing alloy for journal bearings
note: Babbitt (1839) patented this bearing alloy: soft at surface, hard at back. Tin-rich alloy (80%+ Sn) poured over steel back; low friction, easy to run in. Critical for railway and steam engine main bearings. Composition varied; high-tin babbitt was superior but expensive.

name: Type metal: lead-tin-antimony for printing type castings
note: Hard but not brittle; slight expansion on cooling to reproduce sharp details in type. Antimony hardening was key discovery (~1400s). Remelting and recasting type was routine; composition drifted but stayed functional.

name: Britannia metal: tin-copper-antimony, tin-spoon alloy
note: 90%+ tin with copper and antimony hardening. Whiter than pewter, harder, silvered or plated for tableware. Named to appeal to empire (1830s+). Competitive with silver plate. Reheating and recasting similar to type metal.

name: German silver (nickel silver): copper-nickel-zinc without silver
note: 60-65% Cu, 15-20% Ni, 20% Zn. White color and tarnish resistance like silver without cost. Chinese paktong (nickel alloy) known since 1200s; European 'German silver' ~1820s. Plated with sterling silver; competed with Sheffield plate.

name: Monel: nickel-copper alloy for corrosion resistance
note: 50-50 Ni-Cu. Superior corrosion resistance in seawater and many chemical environments. Developed by INCO ~1905. Expensive but used for valve stems, pump parts, marine hardware. Castings, forgings, and sheet possible.

name: Invar: nickel-iron for low thermal expansion
note: 35-36% Ni, 64-65% Fe. Thermal expansion near zero around room temperature. Guillaume (1896) discovered this; critical for precision instruments (standards, pendulums). Used for surveying chains and scientific apparatus. Expensive and difficult to machine.

name: Elinvar: nickel-steel for elastic constant independence from temperature
note: Elastic modulus constant with temperature (unlike normal metals). Guillaume (1920s) developed this for watch balances and precision springs. Requires careful composition control and heat treatment. Complex metallurgy; few suppliers.

name: Nichrome: nickel-chromium for high-temperature resistance
note: 80% Ni, 20% Cr. Oxidation resistance to 1100C+. Used for heating elements (toasters, electric furnaces). Albert Porsche developed this ~1905. Wire drawing and forming difficult; oxidation layer protects. Superior to nichrome-iron.

name: Constantan: copper-nickel thermocouple wire with stable EMF
note: 55% Cu, 45% Ni. Thermoelectric properties stable with time; paired with copper for thermocouple. Seebeck effect exploited for temperature measurement. Developed ~1880s for precision thermometry. High electrical resistance.

name: Manganin: copper-manganese-nickel for precision resistors
note: Electrical resistance nearly constant with temperature (unlike copper or nichrome). Used for precision resistance standards and meter resistors. Discovered ~1900; requires careful composition. Wire drawing and annealing critical.

name: Stellite: cobalt-chromium-tungsten hard alloy for cutting tools
note: Elwood Haynes (1912) developed stellite as cast alloy (no sintering). Extremely hard, holds edge to 900C+. Cuts steel rapidly. Casting defects and brittleness limit use vs. sintered carbides, but predates them. Welding tool bits to steel shafts.

name: High speed steel (HSS): tungsten-molybdenum-vanadium tool steel
note: 18-4-1 (W-Mo-V-Co) formula typical. Taylor-White (1900) discovered that high-speed steel can cut steel at 100+ m/min (vs. 20 for carbon steel). Hardness retained above 600C. Red-hard alloy. Quenching and tempering critical; superseded by carbides but still used.

name: Stainless steel, ferritic: chromium steel with delta ferrite structure
note: 13-17% Cr, low C. Ferrite structure (BCC) remains below melting point. Excellent corrosion resistance; magnetic. Used for cutlery, automotive trim. Monnartz (1912) developed this; Porsche earlier dabbled. Brittleness at low temp; hardenable only by cold work.

name: Stainless steel, austenitic: nickel-chromium with FCC structure
note: 304 stainless (18% Cr, 8% Ni, rest Fe) is typical. Austenite (FCC) stable at all temps. Non-magnetic, excellent formability, superior corrosion resistance. Discovered independently by several groups ~1912-1920. Harder to machine than ferritic; requires high-speed tools.

name: Stainless steel, martensitic: high-carbon chromium, hardenable
note: 12-13% Cr, higher C (0.5%+). Hardens by quenching and tempering. Used for cutlery and surgical instruments. Less corrosion resistant than austenitic. Monnartz (1912) developed this series. Tempering temperature critical for balance of hardness and toughness.

name: Silicon steel for transformer cores: reduced iron loss at 50-60 Hz
note: 3-4% silicon, low carbon. Increases resistivity, reducing eddy-current loss; also reduces hysteresis loss (narrower B-H loop). Oriented grain growth (1940s) further reduced losses. Cold rolling and annealing sequence critical. Became standard by 1920 for AC transformers.

name: Hadfield manganese steel: work-hardening steel for severe impact
note: 11-14% Mn, 1% C. Austenitic, very tough, hardens tremendously under impact (work hardening). Used for railway switches, crusher jaws, military armor. Hadfield (1880s) patent; microstructure was mysterious (austenite + brittle carbides plus transformation). Weldable with difficulty.

name: Spring steel: high-carbon, carefully tempered for elastic return
note: 0.5-1.0% C steel, hardened and tempered blue or straw color. Retains yield point elasticity; returns to shape after bending. Watch springs, vehicle suspensions, precision mechanisms all depend. Quality control critical; brittle fracture if over-tempered or under-tempered.

name: Grey cast iron: graphite-rich iron for castings
note: 2-4% C, graphite particles (flakes) in ferrite/pearlite matrix. Lower melting point than steel (1200C), flows well. Graphite acts as internal lubricant; machinable. Weak in tension (brittle), strong in compression. Cylinder blocks, engine beds, pipes. Cooling rate controls structure.

name: White cast iron: hard but brittle, iron carbide dominant
note: Cooled rapidly so cementite (Fe3C) precipitates instead of graphite. Extremely hard but brittle. Used for mill rolls, grinding media. Unmachinable; must be ground. Annealing converts white iron to malleable iron; heat treatment at 900C for days.

name: Malleable cast iron: annealed white iron, ductile
note: White iron reheated to 900C for 50+ hours; carbon atoms aggregate into graphite nodules, cementite dissolves. Matrix becomes ferrite (soft); dramatic ductility increase. Expensive process but enables casting complex shapes that must survive impact (automotive, machinery).

name: Ductile (nodular) cast iron: spheroidal graphite for strength and ductility
note: Adding magnesium or cerium to molten iron forces graphite into spheroids instead of flakes. Tensile strength rivals steel, ductility far exceeds grey iron. Post-1945 development accelerated; by 1950 becoming commercial. Cooling and thermal treatment control structure.

name: Duralumin: aluminum-copper, age-hardened aircraft alloy
note: Wilm's 1906 discovery: 4% Cu in aluminum, solution-treated, then naturally ages over days to weeks. Strength increases 200%. Enables lightweight aircraft (Fokker, early Junkers). Alloy composition closely guarded. Susceptible to stress-corrosion cracking.

name: Aluminum alloy series: systematic development of wrought alloys
note: 2xxx (Cu-hardened), 3xxx (Mn), 5xxx (Mg), 6xxx (Mg-Si), 7xxx (Zn). Each series has dozens of alloys. Post-1920 systematic alloy development by Alcoa, Hydro, others. Property database built. 7075 (high-strength) came late 1930s. Cold work and heat treatment sequences optimized.

name: Magnesium alloys: weight reduction with controlled corrosion
note: Magnesium 2/3 density of aluminum, 1/3 steel. Alloying with aluminum, zinc, manganese improves strength; beryllium suppresses grain growth. Difficult casting (pyrophoric, needs argon protection). Limited commercial use before 1940. Post-WW2 demand for aerospace grew applications.

name: Titanium alloys: high-strength-to-weight for aerospace
note: Alpha alloys (low strength, creep resistant), beta alloys (formable, strength hardenable), alpha-beta (commercial). Ti-6-4 (Ti-6% Al-4% V) became dominant post-1950 jet alloy. Before 1950, only lab quantities. Extremely difficult to process (high reactivity, poor machinability).

name: Earthenware: low-fired, porous ceramic for everyday use
note: Clay fired to 1000-1150C. Porous (absorbs water); quick to make and glaze. Terracotta tradition ancient. Medieval and later earthenware (faience) decorated and glazed. Lead glaze toxic but durable. Still competitive with stoneware for decorative ware.

name: Stoneware: higher-fired, vitrified ceramic for strength
note: Fired to 1200-1300C; clay particles sinter and partially vitrify. Non-porous, stronger than earthenware. Industrial stoneware (crocks, vessels, pipes) common by 1600s. European salt glaze technique (1600s+) waterproofs without lead. Handles thermal shock better.

name: Bone china: high-firing ceramic with calcined bone
note: China clay mixed with calcined animal bone (ash) and feldspathic material. Fired to 1200-1250C. Whiter, stronger, more translucent than porcelain. English invention (Spode, ~1794). More durable than porcelain; popular for tableware. Competitive pricing vs. true porcelain.

name: Silica brick: high-silica refractory for blast furnaces
note: Quartzite or silica sand bonded with silica gel. Fired to 1400-1500C. Melting point >1700C. Alkaline slag attacks it (converts to fayalite). Used for blast furnace arches, steelmaking furnaces. Brick making and kiln placement critical.

name: Magnesite brick: magnesia refractory for basic furnaces
note: Dead-burned magnesite (MgO sintered at 1600C+) pressed into bricks, refired to 1700C+. Resists alkaline slag. Critical for basic converter, open hearth. Expensive and fragile. Requires careful handling and furnace design to avoid spalling.

name: Chromite brick: chromium-iron refractory for extreme duty
note: Chrome ore sintered and pressed into bricks. Resistant to both acidic and alkaline slag; best all-around refractory. Expensive. Used for premium zones in steelmaking furnaces. Melting point >1800C. Late development (1920s+) for critical applications.

name: Alumina: high-purity aluminum oxide ceramic
note: Bauxite refined to Al2O3, pressed and fired to 1600-1800C. Melting point 2072C. Used for refractory linings, catalyst supports, crucibles. High purity enables translucent alumina (later). Pre-1950 mostly opaque and dense. Excellent thermal shock resistance.

name: Carborundum (silicon carbide): ultra-hard ceramic for abrasives
note: Fusing silica and carbon at 2200C (arc furnace) produces SiC. Acheson (1891) discovered this. Extremely hard (9.5 Mohs), melting point 2700C. Used for grinding wheels, cutting tools, crucibles. Brittle; sintered parts used. Major post-1900 industrial abrasive.

name: Cement varieties: Portland and alternatives for construction
note: Cement types: Portland (high strength, rapid set), white, blast furnace (slag-based), pozzolanic (ash-based). Kiln temperature 1450C; clinker ground fine. Hydration strength develops over weeks-months. Composition (lime, silica, alumina ratios) determines properties. Industrial kiln design critical.

name: Lead glass (flint glass): high-refractive-index optical glass
note: Lead oxide 30-40% increases refractive index and reduces dispersion (makes white light). Enables precision lenses without excessive aberrations. Heavy and dense; toxic if mishandled. English development (18th century); craft closely guarded. Grinding and polishing critical.

name: Optical glass: ultra-pure glasses for telescopes and cameras
note: Schott (Germany) systematically developed optical glasses (1880s+). Composition variation (lead, barium, silica ratios) gives different refractive indices and dispersions. Homogeneity critical; striae cause image degradation. State secret; wars fought over access. Zeiss, Leica, Kodak all sourced from Germany.

name: Glass fiber: fine filaments for insulation and reinforcement
note: Drawing molten glass into fine fibers; bundling and binding with resin. Excellent insulation, low density, fire resistant. Industrial production ~1930s (Owens Corning). Pre-1950 mostly laboratory and premium applications. Binding technology critical.

name: Tempered glass: heat-treated for safety and strength
note: Heating annealed glass to 600C+, then rapid air cooling surface. Compressive surface stress and tensile core. Shatters into granules (safe). 3-4x stronger than annealed. Automobile windshields primary use (post-1930). Furnace design and cooling control critical.

name: Laminated glass: bonded layers for shatter resistance
note: Glass sheets bonded with cellulose nitrate or acetate interlayer. Shatters but does not fall apart. Triplex patent (1909). Used for aircraft and automotive safety. Post-WW1 adoption. Adhesive layer must remain flexible and optically clear.

name: Shaft sinking: deep vertical access to ore bodies
note: Hand drilling and blasting to create deep shafts; pumping and ventilation essential. Competing with water ingress and gases. Cornish deep tin mines (1500+ m) demonstrated feasibility. Steam pumps replaced horse gins. Safety lamp for methane.

name: Drifting: horizontal tunneling along ore seams
note: Following ore body laterally. Less energy than shaft sinking. Ventilation and slope critical to drain water. Rock drill advent (1870s) accelerated. Timber support and bolt pattern evolved with experience.

name: Stoping: extracting ore in upward progression from access drifts
note: Removing ore in a planned sequence to minimize collapse and maximize recovery. Timber support (stulls) holds back rock. Different stoping methods: room-and-pillar, long-wall. Safety depends on control and roof support. Ancient mines used simple open stoping; modern methods evolved 1800s+.

name: Timbering: wooden support structures for mine stability
note: Wooden posts, beams, and lagging hold back rock. Design depends on strata and span. Decay, compression, and crushing require replacement and inspection. European timber mining developed detailed standards (16th-18th centuries). Replaceable without stopping production.

name: Safety lamp: detecting and excluding methane and carbon monoxide
note: Davy lamp (1815): candle in fine mesh gauze; methane burns in mesh without igniting air. Flame height/color indicates gas concentration. Later lamps used chemical reactions to detect CO. Saved thousands of lives; essential before electrical lighting.

name: Ventilation: managing air flow for safety and drainage
note: Furnaces draw hot air up main shaft; cool air returns through working levels. Removes methane, heat, dust. Deep mines need forced ventilation (fans). Cornish and German mining engineering advanced this. Natural convection limited to ~500m depth.

name: Pneumatic rock drill: compressed air powered percussion
note: Siméon and Sommeiller (1860s) developed air drill for Alpine tunnels. Hand hammers then competed. Air compressor (steam-driven or water-turbine) provides 6-10 bar. Speeds tunneling 10x. Mine development accelerated post-1870s.

name: Jackhammer: portable pneumatic pick for ore breaking
note: Lighter and more portable than mounted drill. One or two workers operate. Air hose supply from central compressor. Reduces fatigue and increases productivity 5-10x compared to hand picks. Post-1900 adoption widespread.

name: Shot firer: controlled blasting of ore with powder and detonators
note: Drilling holes, charging with black powder (then dynamite), calculating delays between charges to direct rock breakage. Safety fuse and later electric detonators enable sequenced blast. Craft and experience critical; accidents fatal. Replaced hand picking 1800s+.

name: Hydraulic mining: washing ore and overburden with water pressure
note: High-pressure water from elevated reservoirs erodes gold placer deposits (California, 1870s). Nozzles direct flow. Sluices recover gold. Environmentally destructive (sediment); banned in sensitive areas by 1880s. Efficient but limited to near-surface, unconsolidated deposits.

name: Dredging: mechanical extraction of ore from sediment and water
note: Bucket dredges or suction dredges excavate placer deposits. Onboard sluice separates ore. Alluvial tin, gold, diamonds recovered. Post-1890s adoption for marine and riverine deposits. Capital-intensive but high volume. Environmental impact later recognized.

name: Open-cast mining: large surface excavation removing overburden
note: Steam shovels and draglines remove waste rock to expose ore. Capital investment high but recovery complete. Porphyry copper deposits require open-cast (low grade, huge volume). Post-1920 extension of hydraulic mining concepts. Reclamation not considered pre-1950.

name: Crusher: jaw and cone crushers for initial ore size reduction
note: Jaw crusher uses reciprocating plate; cone crusher rolls against conical surface. Reduces 30cm ore to 5cm. Blake jaw crusher (1858) standard. Powered by steam belt drives. Multiple stages and careful gradation optimize later flotation. Capacity tens of tons/day per unit.

name: Ball mill: cylindrical mill with steel balls for fine grinding
note: Rotating cylinder half-full of steel balls; ore enters one end, grinds as balls tumble, exits other end. Produces fine (-200 mesh) powder for flotation or leaching. Scale from lab to 50+ ton/hr industrial. Post-1890 adoption; became bottleneck, then standard.

name: Classifier: hydraulic or mechanical separation by particle size
note: Spiral or cone classifier uses settling rate in water to sort particles. Fine material overflows; coarse returns to mill. Recirculating load optimization improves efficiency. Spline (cone) classifier most common. Automatic return control (no human adjustment needed once set).

name: Thickener: settling and concentration of ore slurry
note: Large shallow tanks allow slurry to settle; overflow water recycled, underflow (slurry) to next process. Cones aid drainage. Flocculant chemicals accelerate settling. Critical for flotation (thickened feed) and counter-current washing. Scale: 50+ meters diameter for large operations.
